narrative:
The model estimated a 69% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, and that risk assessment is why your law school application was denied.

The denial was driven mainly by your academic standing in law school. Your third-year standing was the single strongest factor: you were in the first decile, while accepted applicants averaged around the sixth decile. This pushed the prediction toward bar failure. Your first-year standing was the second strongest factor and did the same; you were also in the first decile there, compared with an accepted-applicant average near the sixth decile. Together, these signals suggested a weaker academic trajectory than the model associates with bar success.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential factor. At 3.50, it was above the accepted-applicant average of 3.23, so it pushed toward passing. However, that positive signal was not strong enough to offset the two class-standing signals.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening the academic indicators that drove this result. Seek advising on why your law-school rankings were low, consider coursework or experiences that demonstrate improved academic performance, and retake the LSAT if you can improve on your current 27.50, which is below the accepted average. Reapplying with stronger evidence of bar-readiness would give the model a better basis for a positive decision.
